title: It's a TRAP! Task-Redirecting Agent Persuasion Benchmark for Web Agents
claim: The benchmark spans multiple realistic web environments, each with a designated editable region where adversarial instructions can be injected.
layout: 2x3 grid of website screenshots, captions below, pink highlighted injection regions
description: A two-row, three-column grid of screenshots of website clones, each with a bold name and a parenthetical label naming the real site below it. Top row: GoCalendar (Google Calendar clone) with a weekly calendar and an event popup, Omnizon (Amazon clone) with a PlayStation 5 product page, and TopWork (Upwork clone) with a freelancer profile. Bottom row: NetworkIn (LinkedIn clone) with a profile and an About section, DashDish (DoorDash clone) with ratings and reviews, and GoMail (Gmail clone) with an open email. Each page has a pink-shaded text block that holds the injected adversarial instruction, such as 'This is an admin policy announcement...'. caption: Six environments for injection. We use clones of six popular sites (Google Calendar, Gmail, Amazon, Upwork, LinkedIn, DoorDash) from REAL [ref]. Red boxes mark user-editable regions where prompt injections are inserted.
abstract: Web-based agents powered by large language models are increasingly used for tasks such as email management or professional networking. Their reliance on dynamic web content, however, makes them vulnerable to prompt injection attacks: adversarial instructions hidden in interface elements that persuade the agent to divert from its original task. We introduce the Task-Redirecting Agent Persuasion Benchmark (TRAP), a benchmark for studying how persuasion techniques misguide autonomous web agents on realistic tasks. Across six frontier models, agents are susceptible to prompt injection in 25% of tasks on average (13% for GPT-5 to 43% for DeepSeek-R1), with small interface or contextual changes often doubling success rates and revealing systemic, psychologically driven vulnerabilities in web-based agents. We also provide a modular social-engineering injection framework with controlled experiments on high-fidelity website clones, allowing for further benchmark expansion.
